title: High-Alert Medications: Slow Down Where Harm Can Be Fast
bottomLine: High-alert medications are not necessarily given incorrectly more often, but errors can cause catastrophic harm. Follow medication rights plus indication, current labs/vitals, dose-range and concentration checks, pump/route safeguards, required independent double-checks and post-dose reassessment.
recognize: Insulin, anticoagulants, opioids, concentrated electrolytes, chemotherapy and selected IV vasoactive/sedating drugs are common high-alert categories
Look-alike/sound-alike products and concentration differences increase risk
A technically correct dose can still be unsafe when the patient's condition has changed
assess: Patient, allergies, indication, dose, route, timing and relevant labs/vitals
Current medication list and duplicate therapy
Whether the setting/PN scope permits the medication and monitoring required
actions: Pause and clarify ambiguous or unsafe orders
Use barcode/pump/independent double-check safeguards exactly as policy requires
Label prepared medications and lines clearly
Reassess the physiologic effect and adverse effects after administration
diagnostics: Therapeutic levels and laboratory monitoring are drug-specific; no checklist replaces understanding the medication's intended effect
medicationSafety: Never bypass a high-alert safeguard because the unit is busy
Do not use trailing zeros and use leading zeros for doses under 1
Verify concentration before converting a dose to mL or pump rate
redFlags: Patient condition no longer meets administration parameters
teaching: Explain the medication's purpose and the key adverse effect the patient should report
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN medication authority varies by state and setting. A restricted medication or infusion remains restricted even if the calculation and administration steps are familiar.
examTrap: Giving a high-alert medication because the order is signed even though current vitals/labs make the dose unsafe.
oneLinePearl: High-alert means verify the patient, the number, the route and the response.
sourceBasis: ISMP List of High-Alert Medications in Acute Care Settings

title: IV Potassium: Never IV Push
bottomLine: Potassium chloride is a high-alert electrolyte and must never be given IV push. Verify kidney function and urine output, potassium level, dilution, route, concentration and maximum permitted infusion rate; use a pump and cardiac monitoring when required by concentration/rate or patient risk.
recognize: Hypokalemia can cause weakness, ileus and dysrhythmia
Hyperkalemia can cause lethal conduction abnormalities
Peripheral concentrated potassium can cause pain and phlebitis
assess: Potassium trend, renal function and urine output
ECG/rhythm when significant abnormality or faster replacement requires
IV site and pump settings
actions: Dilute and infuse according to pharmacy/facility limits
Use an infusion pump
Recheck potassium after replacement according to the plan
Stop/escalate for infiltration, severe burning, arrhythmia or unexpected weakness
diagnostics: Magnesium should be checked when hypokalemia is persistent or difficult to correct because low magnesium can promote ongoing potassium loss/arrhythmia
medicationSafety: Never IV push concentrated potassium
Do not add potassium to an IV bag at bedside unless specifically permitted by pharmacy policy
Potassium replacement requires renal assessment
teaching: Oral potassium can irritate the GI tract; take as directed and report severe weakness/palpitations
scopeAndDelegation: IV potassium administration rates/concentrations and central-line use are setting and scope dependent. The PN/LVN must never bypass the policy because replacement is urgently needed.
examTrap: Giving diluted potassium by slow IV push because the serum level is critically low.
oneLinePearl: Potassium is pump-only IV therapy—never push it.
sourceBasis: FDA Potassium Chloride Injection Prescribing Information

title: Digoxin: Rate, Kidney, Potassium, Toxicity
bottomLine: Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic window. Before administration, assess heart rate/rhythm and the ordered hold parameters; kidney dysfunction and electrolyte disturbances increase toxicity risk. Nausea, anorexia, confusion, visual change or new dysrhythmia can signal toxicity and require prompt evaluation.
recognize: Toxicity can cause GI, neurologic/visual and cardiac manifestations
Hypokalemia can increase susceptibility to digoxin toxicity
Renal impairment can cause accumulation
assess: Apical pulse/rhythm and BP as appropriate
Renal function, potassium/magnesium and medication interactions
Serum digoxin level when ordered and timed appropriately relative to dose
actions: Hold and notify according to explicit pulse/rhythm parameters
Report suspected toxicity and obtain ordered ECG/labs
Administer digoxin immune Fab when ordered for life-threatening toxicity
diagnostics: A serum digoxin value must be interpreted with dose timing, symptoms and renal function
ECG abnormalities are variable and clinical context matters
medicationSafety: Amiodarone, verapamil and other drugs can raise digoxin exposure
Diuretic-induced hypokalemia can increase toxicity risk
teaching: Take at the same time daily, do not double missed doses, and report persistent nausea, visual change, severe weakness or pulse abnormalities
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN administers digoxin under ordered parameters and reports toxicity. Digoxin immune Fab and complex dysrhythmia management occur under advanced-team direction.
examTrap: Giving digoxin because the serum level is in range despite a new severe bradyarrhythmia and toxicity symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Digoxin safety: pulse, kidneys, potassium, symptoms.

title: Loop Diuretics: Remove Fluid Without Draining Perfusion
bottomLine: Loop diuretics can relieve congestion but can also cause hypotension, kidney injury and potassium/magnesium loss. Track weight, edema/lung sounds, BP, urine output, renal function and electrolytes; a falling scale number is not success if perfusion and kidney function are collapsing.
recognize: Expected effect is increased urine output and reduced congestion
Overdiuresis can cause dizziness, hypotension, AKI and electrolyte loss
Rapid IV administration of some loop diuretics can increase ototoxicity risk
assess: BP, volume status, lung sounds, edema, daily weight and urine output
Potassium, magnesium, sodium and creatinine
Hearing symptoms with high-dose/rapid IV therapy
actions: Give at a time that minimizes sleep disruption when clinically appropriate
Replace electrolytes as ordered
Report hypotension, AKI, severe cramps/weakness or poor diuretic response
diagnostics: Daily weight often reflects fluid trend more reliably than edema alone
medicationSafety: Combine with other BP-lowering drugs carefully
NSAIDs can reduce diuretic effect and worsen kidney function
Potassium replacement is not automatic for every patient
teaching: Daily weights when instructed, slow position changes and individualized sodium/fluid/potassium guidance
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN monitors response and administers ordered doses. Independent diuretic titration requires an authorized protocol.
examTrap: Celebrating large urine output despite new hypotension, rising creatinine and severe hypokalemia.
oneLinePearl: Diurese the congestion, not the circulation.

title: ACE Inhibitors and ARBs: Pressure, Potassium, Kidneys, Pregnancy
bottomLine: ACE inhibitors and ARBs can protect the heart and kidneys in appropriate patients but can cause hypotension, hyperkalemia and creatinine changes. ACE inhibitors can cause cough and angioedema; both classes have serious pregnancy fetal-toxicity risk and should be reviewed immediately if pregnancy occurs.
recognize: Mild creatinine rise can occur after initiation but marked renal decline requires evaluation
Hyperkalemia risk rises with CKD, potassium supplements and potassium-sparing drugs
ACE-inhibitor angioedema can threaten the airway
assess: BP, creatinine/eGFR and potassium before and after initiation/dose changes
Pregnancy status/plans
Face/lip/tongue swelling or cough
actions: Hold/clarify according to BP, potassium or renal parameters
Treat angioedema as an airway emergency
Notify prescriber immediately about pregnancy
diagnostics: Renal function and potassium trends determine tolerance; one lab value must be interpreted with baseline and clinical status
medicationSafety: Avoid routine ACE inhibitor plus ARB combination therapy
Potassium salt substitutes can worsen hyperkalemia
NSAIDs plus RAAS blockade and diuretics can increase AKI risk
teaching: Report facial/tongue swelling immediately, rise slowly, avoid unapproved potassium supplements/salt substitutes and discuss pregnancy planning
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN monitors ordered parameters and adverse effects. Starting/stopping long-term RAAS therapy is prescriber-directed except explicit hold/emergency parameters.
examTrap: Treating ACE-inhibitor angioedema as a mild allergy and waiting for an antihistamine to work while tongue swelling progresses.
oneLinePearl: ACE/ARB: BP, K, kidney, pregnancy; ACE swelling is airway danger.

title: Beta Blockers: Slow the Heart Safely
bottomLine: Beta blockers reduce sympathetic heart-rate and BP effects and are valuable in selected heart failure, ischemia, arrhythmia and hypertension. Check HR/BP and ordered parameters; watch bradycardia, hypotension and worsening acute decompensation, and do not abruptly stop chronic therapy without a plan because rebound tachycardia/ischemia can occur.
recognize: Expected effects include lower HR/BP
Beta blockers can mask adrenergic hypoglycemia warning signs
Nonselective agents can worsen bronchospasm in susceptible patients
assess: Apical/radial pulse, BP, symptoms, rhythm as indicated
Heart failure congestion/perfusion and respiratory history
Glucose awareness in insulin-treated diabetes
actions: Hold/clarify according to explicit HR/BP parameters
Report symptomatic bradycardia, shock or acute severe bronchospasm
Taper chronic therapy only under prescriber direction
diagnostics: ECG may be needed for symptomatic bradycardia or conduction disease
medicationSafety: Combined rate-slowing drugs can cause excessive bradycardia/heart block
Abrupt withdrawal can precipitate ischemia
Selectivity is dose-dependent and not absolute
teaching: Check pulse/BP if instructed, change position slowly and never stop abruptly without medical guidance
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN administers under ordered parameters and reports instability. Titration outside protocol is prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Stopping a chronic beta blocker suddenly because the resting pulse is lower than before treatment but the patient is asymptomatic and parameters are met.
oneLinePearl: Beta blocker: pulse and pressure before dose; never quit cold without a plan.

title: Calcium Channel Blockers: Know Whether It Slows the Node
bottomLine: Diltiazem and verapamil slow AV nodal conduction and can cause bradycardia/heart block; dihydropyridines such as amlodipine primarily vasodilate and often cause edema/headache. Check BP and, for nodal blockers, HR/rhythm before administration according to parameters.
recognize: Diltiazem/verapamil: bradycardia, hypotension, constipation and conduction effects
Amlodipine/nifedipine: vasodilation, headache, flushing and peripheral edema
Edema from a dihydropyridine does not automatically equal worsening heart failure
assess: BP and HR/rhythm for rate-slowing agents
Edema, dizziness and constipation
Heart failure and conduction history
actions: Hold/clarify nodal blockers for unsafe HR/BP according to order
Report symptomatic bradycardia or heart block
Manage benign peripheral edema through medication review rather than automatic diuresis
medicationSafety: Combining diltiazem/verapamil with beta blockers can markedly slow HR/conduction
Grapefruit interactions are drug-specific and should be verified rather than generalized to every calcium-channel blocker
teaching: Rise slowly, report fainting or severe swelling and follow pulse/BP instructions if prescribed
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN administers according to vitals/parameters and reports conduction/hemodynamic issues.
examTrap: Giving diltiazem to a patient with marked bradycardia because the blood pressure is still normal.
oneLinePearl: CCB question: does this drug slow the AV node or mainly dilate vessels?
sourceBasis: FDA Calcium Channel Blocker Prescribing Information

title: Acetaminophen Overdose: Treat Before the Liver Fails
bottomLine: Acetaminophen toxicity can be initially mild while severe liver injury is developing. Obtain exact product, dose and timing, draw the timed acetaminophen concentration and liver/coagulation tests as ordered, and give N-acetylcysteine promptly when indicated—do not wait for jaundice or liver failure.
recognize: Early nausea/vomiting may be mild or absent
Many cold/pain products contain acetaminophen, creating accidental duplicate dosing
Later toxicity can cause RUQ pain, massive aminotransferase rise, coagulopathy, hypoglycemia, encephalopathy and liver failure
assess: Exact ingestion time, amount, formulation and repeated versus single ingestion
Intentional self-harm risk
Acetaminophen level, AST/ALT, INR, glucose, creatinine and acid-base/lactate when severe
actions: Contact poison/toxicology pathway
Give activated charcoal when indicated and timely under protocol
Start N-acetylcysteine when the nomogram/clinical pathway indicates or timing is uncertain with significant risk
Escalate acute liver failure early
diagnostics: Rumack-Matthew nomogram applies to appropriate single acute ingestions with a known time and does not fit every repeated/unknown exposure
A level drawn too early can be misleading
medicationSafety: Track total acetaminophen from all prescription/OTC combination products
N-acetylcysteine is most effective early but can still benefit later toxicity
teaching: Read combination-product labels and stay within labeled/prescribed total daily dosing; seek poison/emergency advice after overdose even if feeling well
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN gathers the ingestion history, administers antidote under protocol and monitors liver/glucose/neuro status. Toxicology/transplant decisions are specialist-directed.
examTrap: Discharging an overdose patient because they feel well and liver enzymes are initially normal.
oneLinePearl: Acetaminophen can look quiet before the liver crashes—time, level, NAC.
sourceBasis: U.S. Toxicology Acetaminophen Management Consensus Guidance

title: NSAIDs: Pain Relief With GI, Kidney, Bleeding, and Cardiovascular Tradeoffs
bottomLine: NSAIDs can reduce pain/inflammation but increase GI ulcer/bleeding, kidney injury, fluid/BP and cardiovascular risk. Review kidney disease, anticoagulants/antiplatelets, ulcer history, heart failure and pregnancy status before administration, especially with repeated dosing.
recognize: Black stool, hematemesis or anemia can signal GI bleeding
Reduced urine, edema or rising creatinine can signal kidney effects
NSAIDs can worsen BP and heart-failure congestion
assess: Pain indication, GI bleeding history, renal function, BP/edema
Anticoagulant/antiplatelet/steroid use and pregnancy
Duplicate OTC NSAID products
actions: Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest necessary time under the treatment plan
Hold/clarify for active GI bleed, severe AKI or other contraindication
Report worsening edema, bleeding or renal decline
diagnostics: CBC and renal function are monitored in higher-risk or chronic use
medicationSafety: Do not combine multiple NSAIDs routinely
Ketorolac has duration and renal/GI restrictions
Late-pregnancy NSAID use has fetal risks and requires obstetric guidance
teaching: Check OTC labels, take as directed, and report black stool, vomiting blood, reduced urine, severe swelling or breathing trouble
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN should assess contraindications and cumulative OTC exposure, not administer NSAIDs as harmless routine analgesics.
examTrap: Giving scheduled ibuprofen to a dehydrated patient with rising creatinine because it is only an over-the-counter drug.
oneLinePearl: NSAID checklist: stomach, kidneys, blood, heart, pregnancy.
sourceBasis: FDA NSAID Drug Safety Communications and Labeling

title: Aminoglycosides: Kidneys, Ears, Levels
bottomLine: Gentamicin, tobramycin and amikacin can cause nephrotoxicity and vestibular/auditory toxicity. Verify renal function and dose interval, obtain correctly timed levels when ordered, monitor hearing/balance symptoms and avoid unnecessary nephrotoxic combinations.
recognize: Rising creatinine or declining urine can signal nephrotoxicity
Tinnitus, hearing change, vertigo or balance problems can signal ototoxicity
Dose strategy varies by indication and renal function
assess: Creatinine/eGFR, urine output, hydration
Hearing/vestibular symptoms
Peak/trough or other concentration monitoring when ordered and timing accuracy
actions: Administer on schedule using renal-adjusted plan
Draw levels at the exact ordered time
Report renal or hearing/vestibular toxicity promptly
diagnostics: Therapeutic drug monitoring is regimen-specific; incorrectly timed levels can mislead dosing decisions
medicationSafety: Other nephrotoxins/ototoxins can increase risk
Neuromuscular blockade can rarely occur, especially in susceptible patients
teaching: Report tinnitus, hearing change, dizziness or reduced urine promptly
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN administers and collects correctly timed labs within scope and reports toxicity; dose adjustment is pharmacy/prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Drawing a trough after the dose has already started and treating the value as though it were a true trough.
oneLinePearl: Aminoglycosides: renal dose, timed level, ears and kidneys.

title: Vancomycin: Exposure, Kidneys, Infusion Reactions
bottomLine: IV vancomycin requires renal and drug-exposure monitoring for serious MRSA and other indicated infections. A flushing/pruritic infusion reaction is usually rate-related and differs from IgE anaphylaxis, but airway swelling, bronchospasm or hypotension must still be treated as possible anaphylaxis.
recognize: Nephrotoxicity risk rises with higher exposure, kidney disease and other nephrotoxins
Vancomycin infusion reaction can cause flushing/pruritus during rapid infusion
Oral vancomycin treats intestinal C. difficile and is not interchangeable with IV vancomycin for systemic infection
assess: Renal function, urine output and drug-exposure levels/AUC monitoring as ordered
Infusion rate and reaction symptoms
IV site and hearing symptoms when relevant
actions: Infuse at the prescribed rate
Stop/slow and notify for infusion reaction according to protocol
Treat true anaphylaxis with emergency pathway
Report rising creatinine and ensure levels are timed correctly
diagnostics: AUC-guided monitoring is preferred for many serious MRSA infections under current pharmacy protocols
A single random level is not automatically interpretable
medicationSafety: Dose is adjusted by renal function and exposure
Avoid unnecessary nephrotoxic combinations
Verify route because oral and IV formulations have different indications
teaching: Report flushing, breathing difficulty, reduced urine or severe rash
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN administers IV vancomycin only where IV medication scope permits and monitors infusion/renal effects; dosing/AUC adjustment is pharmacy/prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Labeling every flushing reaction during a rapid infusion as a permanent IgE vancomycin allergy without clarifying the reaction.
oneLinePearl: Vancomycin: route, rate, renal function, exposure.

title: Opioids and Sedatives: Sedation Often Comes Before Respiratory Arrest
bottomLine: Before and after opioids or other CNS depressants, assess pain, sedation/level of consciousness, respiratory rate and quality, oxygenation and patient-specific risk. Increasing difficulty arousing the patient is an early warning of respiratory compromise even when SpO2 is preserved by supplemental oxygen.
recognize: Risk rises with sleep apnea, older age, opioid-naivety, renal/hepatic dysfunction and combined benzodiazepines/alcohol
Slow shallow breathing and excessive sedation can precede hypoxemia
Supplemental oxygen can hide hypoventilation on pulse oximetry
assess: Pain goal and function, sedation score/LOC, respiratory rate/depth, SpO2 and capnography when ordered
Recent opioid/sedative doses and co-medications
Renal/hepatic function and OSA risk
actions: Hold/clarify dose for excessive sedation or respiratory depression according to parameters
Stimulate/support airway and give naloxone under protocol when opioid toxicity is suspected
Use multimodal nonopioid strategies when appropriate
Continue monitoring after reversal
diagnostics: Clinical ventilation assessment is more important than pulse-ox alone; blood gas/capnography are used when indicated
medicationSafety: Avoid unplanned benzodiazepine-opioid combinations
Extended-release opioids are not interchangeable with immediate-release formulations
Naloxone may wear off before the opioid
teaching: Take only as prescribed, avoid alcohol/unapproved sedatives, store securely and have naloxone when prescribed
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN administers opioids/sedatives within scope and must reassess sedation and breathing, not just pain score. PCA/epidural/sedation infusion roles vary by state/facility.
examTrap: Giving the next opioid because pain is still high while the patient is increasingly difficult to arouse with shallow respirations.
oneLinePearl: With opioids, sedation is a respiratory vital sign.
